en: To come before in time; to precede
hook: ANTE = before. Dated BEFORE.
story: Antedate. On a school trip to Mahasthangarh in Bogura, Imran's class walked among ancient brick walls and the ruins of a city more than two thousand years old. Their guide pointed out that this city antedates the Mughal Empire by well over a thousand years, and even antedates most of the famous kingdoms they had studied. To antedate is to come before in time. Ante means before, as in antecedent. Its synonyms are predate and precede.

gre.s: Recent excavations suggest that farming in the valley may ____ the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years.
gre.clue: the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years

en: To send someone away officially as punishment; to get rid of
hook: BANISH: make them VANISH.
story: Banish. In the old epic, a jealous queen tricked the king into banishing his own son, the prince, to the forest for fourteen years. The prince left the palace with nothing but his wife and brother. Centuries later, Mitu banished her phone from her bedroom every night to sleep better, and it worked. To banish is to send someone away officially as punishment, or to get rid of something. You can banish fears and doubts too. Think: make them vanish.

gre.s: Determined to ____ every trace of the old regime, the new government renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks.
gre.clue: renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks

en: To restrain or control; also, to show resentment or anger
bn: সংযত করা; লাগাম টানা, ক্ষোভ প্রকাশ করা
hook: BRIDLE: the straps on a horse's head that hold it back.
story: Bridle. At the market, a shopkeeper insulted Arif's mother over a few taka. Arif felt his face burn and his fists tighten. But he took a long breath, bridled his anger, paid, and walked away calmly. A bridle is the leather harness used to control a horse. To bridle is to restrain or control. Tricky: bridle can also mean to bristle with anger: "She bridled at the insult." Read the context carefully.

gre.s: The coach urged his young striker to ____ his temper, since another red card would mean missing the final.
gre.clue: since another red card would mean missing the final

en: To act according to a rule, request, or command
hook: COMPLY: COMPLETE what's asked.
story: Comply. The new law said that every bus must have a speed limiter and that drivers must rest after six hours. Most transport companies complied within a month, installing the devices and changing shifts. Three companies ignored the law and were fined heavily. To comply is to act according to a rule, request, or command. Compliance with safety rules keeps everyone alive. Think: complete what was asked.

gre.s: Companies that refuse to ____ with the new environmental regulations will face heavy fines and possible closure.
gre.clue: will face heavy fines and possible closure

en: Sad and disappointed
hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
story: Crestfallen. Tanvir had studied for eight months for the scholarship exam. When the results were posted, he searched the list three times. His name was not there. He had missed the cut-off by two marks. He walked out with his head down, shoulders slumped, unable to speak. He was crestfallen: sad and deeply disappointed. Picture a proud rooster whose bright crest has suddenly drooped. It is the opposite of elated.

gre.s: The usually confident candidate looked ____ as the results came in, his campaign having fallen far short of expectations.
gre.clue: having fallen far short of expectations

en: To reduce or cut short
hook: CUR-TAIL: cut the TAIL short.
story: Curtail. The school's annual sports day began brightly. Then the radio announced an approaching cyclone. The principal stopped the races after only two events and sent everyone home. The day had been curtailed: cut short. That year, the government also curtailed its spending, reducing budgets for new buildings. To curtail is to reduce or cut short. Curfews curtail freedom of movement. Think: cutting the tail short.

gre.s: Fearing a budget shortfall, the university was forced to ____ its research programs, eliminating nearly a third of them.
gre.clue: eliminating nearly a third of them

en: To make clear; to explain
hook: E-LUCID-ATE: make it LUCID (clear).
story: Elucidate. Half the biology class looked confused about photosynthesis. Their teacher put down the textbook, drew a simple picture of a leaf, and added three arrows: sunlight in, water from the roots, and sugar and oxygen out. "That is all it is." Suddenly every face relaxed. She had elucidated it: made it clear and explained it. E means out, lucid means clear: bringing clarity out. Good writers elucidate rather than confuse.

gre.s: In an appendix, the author attempts to ____ the more technical concepts for readers without a background in physics.
gre.clue: for readers without a background in physics

en: To escape or avoid, especially by cleverness or trickery
hook: EVADE: like an EVASIVE dodge.
story: Evade. For ten years, a wealthy businessman evaded paying taxes by hiding money in foreign bank accounts and fake companies. When journalists finally asked him about it at a press conference, he evaded the question too, talking at length about his charity work instead. To evade is to escape or avoid something, especially by cleverness or trickery. Tax evasion is illegal; tax avoidance can be legal. An evasive answer dodges the question.

gre.s: The fugitive managed to ____ capture for nearly a decade by moving constantly and using a series of false identities.
gre.clue: by moving constantly and using a series of false identities

en: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective
hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
story: Feckless. The new office manager never made decisions, never answered emails, and disappeared whenever a problem arose. When projects failed, he blamed his team. When clients complained, he forwarded the emails without comment. After six months, staff simply stopped asking him anything. He was feckless: irresponsible, lacking initiative, and ineffective. Feck is an old Scottish word for effect. Feckless means without any effect at all.

gre.s: Voters grew frustrated with the ____ government, which announced ambitious plans every year but never carried any of them out.
gre.clue: never carried any of them out

en: To become worse, especially through neglect; to rot
hook: FESTER: like an untreated wound that grows worse.
story: Fester. Rafi cut his foot on a rusty nail and ignored it. A week later the small cut had festered: red, swollen, infected, and painful. He spent three days on antibiotics. His anger toward his brother was the same: never discussed, just buried, slowly growing worse for years until one small comment caused an explosion. To fester is to become worse, especially through neglect. Unresolved problems fester. Wounds fester when untreated.

gre.s: Left unaddressed, the resentment among the workers continued to ____, eventually erupting in a bitter strike.
gre.clue: eventually erupting in a bitter strike

en: Attacking cherished beliefs or established traditions
hook: ICON-O-CLAST: one who smashes ICONS.
story: Iconoclastic. The young director's first film questioned everything society held sacred: arranged marriages, exam rankings, hero worship of politicians, even the sanctity of family dinners. Some viewers walked out; others called it brilliant. Critics called it iconoclastic: attacking cherished beliefs and established traditions. Originally, iconoclasts literally smashed religious images, or icons. Today, an iconoclastic thinker shatters accepted ideas.

gre.s: The economist's ____ theories, which challenged nearly every assumption of her field, were initially ridiculed but are now widely accepted.
gre.clue: challenged nearly every assumption of her field

en: To confine or imprison within walls
hook: IM-MURE: 'mur' is wall (mural). Walled in.
story: Immure. In old legends, a cruel king punished his enemies by immuring them inside the palace walls, sealing them in with bricks. Centuries later, Nadia immured herself in her bedroom for the whole month before her exam, coming out only for meals and the bathroom. Her family slid tea under the door. To immure is to confine or imprison within walls. Mur means wall, as in mural. Think: walled in.

gre.s: Rather than mingling with other scholars, the reclusive historian chose to ____ himself in the archive for months at a time.
gre.clue: Rather than mingling with other scholars

en: To create or perform without preparation
hook: IMPROVISE: IM-PRO-VISE, not foreseen (pro-vise), done on the spot.
story: Improvise. Halfway through Sara's big presentation, the projector died. Two hundred people stared at a blank screen. Sara paused, smiled, picked up a marker, and drew her charts on the whiteboard from memory, telling the story of her research as she went. The audience loved it even more. She had improvised: created or performed something without preparation. Jazz musicians improvise solos. Improvise means unforeseen, done on the spot.

gre.s: When the main speaker failed to arrive, the host was forced to ____, delivering a twenty-minute talk with no notes at all.
gre.clue: with no notes at all

en: To restrain, hinder, or prevent
hook: INHIBIT: keeps you IN, holding you back.
story: Inhibit. Tanvir knew every answer in English class, but fear of making mistakes inhibited him from speaking. Every time he opened his mouth, his throat closed. His teacher started a small conversation club, and slowly he found his voice. To inhibit is to restrain, hinder, or prevent. Certain medicines inhibit the growth of bacteria. Inhibitions are feelings that hold you back socially. Think: keeps you in.

gre.s: Researchers hope the new compound will ____ the growth of tumors without damaging healthy tissue.
gre.clue: without damaging healthy tissue

en: Impossible to understand or interpret
hook: IN-SCRUTABLE: can't be SCRUTINIZED.
story: Inscrutable. At the national poker tournament, the final player sat absolutely still. No smile. No frown. No twitch. Not even a blink. Opponents studied his face for clues and found nothing. Was he holding a perfect hand or bluffing with nothing at all? He won the tournament without anyone ever reading him. His face was inscrutable: impossible to understand or interpret. In means not, scrutable means able to be scrutinized. Synonym: enigmatic.

gre.s: The cat's ____ expression gave no hint of whether it was about to purr contentedly or lash out with its claws.
gre.clue: gave no hint

en: To treat someone as a celebrity
bn: বীরের মতো সম্মান করা; তারকা বানিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
story: Lionize. A shy girl from a fishing village in Bhola won the international mathematics olympiad. Within a week she was everywhere: TV interviews, newspaper covers, reception ceremonies, a meeting with the prime minister. People asked for her autograph in the street. She was lionized: treated as a celebrity and hero. Picture being treated like the lion, king of the jungle. Societies often lionize their heroes, though sometimes the wrong ones.

gre.s: Although the press rushed to ____ the scientist after her discovery, she found the constant attention exhausting and retreated from public life.
gre.clue: she found the constant attention exhausting

en: Dull and tedious because of lack of variety
hook: MONO-TONE: one tone, over and over.
story: Monotonous. At the factory, Kamal's job was to put the same bolt into the same hole on the same machine part. Eight thousand times a day. Six days a week. Same sound, same motion, same view. After a month, he felt his mind switching off by ten in the morning. His work was monotonous: dull and tedious because nothing ever changed. Mono means one, tone means sound: one single note, forever.

gre.s: The ____ landscape, mile after mile of identical wheat fields, made the long drive feel endless.
gre.clue: mile after mile of identical wheat fields

en: Strange or unusual; belonging exclusively to one person or place
hook: PECULIAR: PECULIAR things are PECULIARLY yours.
story: Peculiar. When Mitu walked into the kitchen, there was a peculiar smell: burnt sugar, wet socks, and something like cinnamon. Her brother was attempting his first cake. Mitu's family also has a peculiar habit: everyone says "Bismillah" before switching on the generator. Peculiar means strange and unusual, or belonging distinctively to one person or place. A custom peculiar to Sylhet is found only there.

gre.s: The custom of exchanging salt as a gift is ____ to the region and is unknown even in neighboring provinces.
gre.clue: unknown even in neighboring provinces

en: To plan something, often a crime, in advance
hook: PRE-MEDITATE: MEDITATE on it BEFORE doing it.
story: Premeditate. The jewellery shop robbery looked spontaneous. But police discovered that the thieves had watched the shop for six weeks, recorded the guard's shift times, bought masks in advance, and even timed the traffic lights outside. The crime had been premeditated: planned beforehand. Pre means before, meditate means think deeply. Premeditated crimes are punished more severely than crimes of passion, committed in a moment of anger.

gre.s: The prosecution argued that the defendant had taken weeks to ____ the crime, pointing to receipts for tools bought a month earlier.
gre.clue: pointing to receipts for tools bought a month earlier

en: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful; shamelessly immoral
hook: PROFLIGATE: PRO at wasting.
story: Profligate. When the old zamindar died, his son inherited a fortune. Within three years it was gone: luxury cars, endless parties, gambling in Singapore, gifts for friends he barely knew. When the money ran out, so did the friends. He was profligate: recklessly extravagant and wasteful. Profligate can also mean shamelessly immoral. Synonyms: prodigal, spendthrift. Think: a pro at wasting everything.

gre.s: Critics attacked the government's ____ spending, noting that it had borrowed billions to build a stadium that would rarely be used.
gre.clue: borrowed billions to build a stadium that would rarely be used

en: To restore friendly relations; to make two things consistent
hook: RE-CONCILE: bring back to COUNCIL, back together.
story: Reconcile. Two brothers in Jessore had not spoken for ten years after a dispute over land. When their mother fell gravely ill, both came to the hospital. They stood on opposite sides of her bed. She took one hand of each and joined them together. That night, the brothers hugged and cried. They reconciled: restored friendly relations. Reconcile also means to make two things consistent: accountants reconcile bank statements so the numbers match.

gre.s: The theory struggles to ____ two sets of findings that appear to contradict each other.
gre.clue: that appear to contradict each other

en: To improve by making small changes; to remove impurities
hook: RE-FINE: make it FINE again and again.
story: Refine. Rafi wrote his statement of purpose in one evening. Then he refined it: twelve drafts over three weeks, cutting weak sentences, sharpening examples, and replacing vague words with precise ones. The final version was half the length and twice as powerful. To refine is to improve something through small changes, or to remove impurities. Factories refine sugar until it is pure white. Refined manners are polished and elegant.

gre.s: Over decades, the craftsmen continued to ____ their techniques, gradually eliminating flaws until their porcelain was the finest in the world.
gre.clue: gradually eliminating flaws

en: To voluntarily give up or let go
hook: RELINQUISH: RELease and finISH.
story: Relinquish. For fifty years, Mr. Haque ran the textile company he had founded with a single sewing machine. At seventy-five, he finally relinquished control to his daughter, signing the papers with a trembling hand. It was the hardest thing he had ever done. To relinquish is to voluntarily give up or let go of something: power, a claim, a position, or your grip on a rope. Think: release and finish.

gre.s: The aging dictator refused to ____ power, even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin.
gre.clue: even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin

en: To think deeply about something
hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
story: Ruminate. Sitting on the steps of the river ghat at dusk, Tanvir ruminated on his future. Stay in Bangladesh near his family, or go abroad for a better career? He turned the question over and over for hours, chewing on every possibility. To ruminate is to think deeply about something, for a long time. Cows ruminate too: they chew their cud again and again. Too much rumination on past mistakes leads to anxiety.

gre.s: Instead of acting decisively, the general would ____ for days over every decision, by which time the opportunity had usually passed.
gre.clue: Instead of acting decisively

en: Nervous and easily frightened; unpredictable
hook: SKITTISH: like a SKITTERING kitten, jumps at every sound.
story: Skittish. Joya tried for weeks to befriend a stray kitten outside her building. It was skittish: whenever someone moved, even slightly, it bolted under a car. A door slamming three floors away would send it running. Investors can be skittish too, selling all their shares at the first sign of bad news. Skittish means nervous, easily frightened, and unpredictable. Picture a kitten skittering away at every sound.

gre.s: The horse was so ____ that the slightest rustle in the bushes would send it bolting across the field.
gre.clue: the slightest rustle in the bushes would send it bolting

en: More than needed; unnecessary
hook: SUPER-FLUOUS: flows (flu) OVER (super) the top.
story: Superfluous. Arif's first draft described the building as "very extremely big huge enormous." His editor deleted four words and left one: "enormous." The rest were superfluous: more than needed, unnecessary. Super means over, fluous means flowing: flowing over the top of the cup. A superfluous remark adds nothing to a conversation. Good GRE essays contain no superfluous words.

gre.s: The editor cut several paragraphs that she considered ____, since they merely repeated points made earlier in the chapter.
gre.clue: merely repeated points made earlier

en: Giving a brief general summary or overview
hook: SYN-OPTIC: seeing (optic) everything together (syn). A SYNOPSIS.
story: Synoptic. On the first day of the semester, Professor Rahman did not start with details. Instead, she spent ten minutes drawing one large diagram on the board, showing the five main topics of the course and how they connected. For the first time, students saw the big picture before diving in. Her overview was synoptic: giving a brief, general summary. Syn means together, optic means seeing. A synopsis summarizes a film's plot.

gre.s: The chapter offers a ____ view of the war, condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages.
gre.clue: condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages

en: Complete with regard to every detail
hook: THOROUGH: goes THROUGH everything.
story: Thorough. Before submitting her university application, Mitu printed everything and checked it line by line: every document, every date, every spelling, every signature. It took a whole day. She found two small mistakes, a wrong year and a misspelled professor's name, that could have cost her admission. Her check was thorough: complete with regard to every detail. Its opposite is cursory. Think: it goes through everything.

gre.s: Unlike the hasty earlier investigation, the new inquiry was ____, interviewing every witness and examining every document.
gre.clue: interviewing every witness and examining every document

en: Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
hook: VISIONARY: has a VISION of the future.
story: Visionary. Fifty years ago, a village schoolteacher in Gopalganj stood in an empty field and announced, "One day, a university will stand here." People laughed. He raised money for decades, one taka at a time. Today, that university has ten thousand students. He was a visionary: someone who thinks about the future with imagination and wisdom. Depending on context, visionary can also mean idealistic but impractical.

gre.s: Dismissed in her own time as a dreamer, the urban planner is now hailed as a ____ whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities.
gre.clue: whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities

en: Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully
hook: VOCI-FEROUS: a VOICE that's FEROCIOUS.
story: Vociferous. When the cricket board dropped the country's favourite batsman, the fans were not quiet about it. They shouted outside the board's office, chanted in the streets, flooded social media with angry posts, and called radio shows all day. Their criticism was vociferous: expressing opinions loudly and forcefully. Vox means voice, ferous means carrying: a voice carried far. A vociferous critic makes sure everyone hears.

gre.s: The proposal met with ____ opposition from residents, who packed the town hall and shouted down every speaker in favor.
gre.clue: shouted down every speaker in favor
